title: Flock says it's transparent. Its own customers are told to keep quiet.
body: The Flock pitch is safety plus accountability. New reporting shows a surveillance network that cops are told to hide. 404 Media obtained a Wapello County, Iowa policy document that instructs deputies in all caps, "DO NOT MENTION ALPR USAGE TO THE OCCUPANTS OF THE VEHICLE. DO NOT MENTION ALPR USAGE IN YOUR REPORT OR COMPLAINT UNLESS ABSOLUTELY NECESSARY." When they do have to write it down, they are coached to call the license plate cameras "county resources." Earlier this year 404 found police in multiple states were told by the FBI and DOJ to be "as vague as permissible" about why they run Flock searches.

This is not a few bad apples. The Lever finds dozens of officers accused of improperly accessing these cameras. 404 also published a leaked Flock coaching guide that teaches cops how to sell the tech to their own city councils, under the banner "own the narrative." A former Flock salesman, Jonathan Paz, quit and put it simply. They lied.

So you have a company that sells itself on transparency, quietly opts towns into a national camera network, then trains the officers using it to talk around it. Flock runs roughly 120,000 cameras across the country. When the safest move is to hide that you used a tool, that tells you what it is actually for.
